h:
If you have spent any time in Western churches or online Christian spaces, you have seen what modern Christianity has become skilled at producing.

Endless devotionals. Prophecy charts. Buy my book. Subscribe here. Join there. The rapture is this year. Another conference. Another reading plan. Another stream of Christian content asking for your attention.

But tell me honestly: when was the last time you heard a serious sermon on self-control?

When was the last time a preacher stood before young men and said with confidence, “Flee sexual immorality”?

When was the last time a church taught believers how to fast, govern appetite, control speech, endure discomfort, resist fantasy, order attention, or bring the body under obedience?

The Bible teaches these things repeatedly. Christ taught them. The apostles taught them. The early Church practiced them.

Yet modern Christianity behaves as though discipline is a side subject, while devotionals, prophecy, reassurance, and religious content fill the shelves.

How did a faith built on denying the flesh become a church governed by appetite?

Grace Trains the Body

Paul does not describe self-control as a personality type.

He names it as fruit of the Spirit:

“But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness, self-control.” - Galatians 5:22–23, BLB

Some people are naturally more organized than others. Some keep schedules easily. Some prefer routines. Biblical self-control reaches deeper than temperament. It is the ordered rule of desire beneath obedience to God. It appears when appetite speaks and the believer refuses to treat appetite as lord.

If self-control is fruit of the Spirit, why is its absence treated as normal church life?

Paul answers another common escape in Titus. Grace does more than forgive the sinner after failure. Grace becomes a teacher:

“For the grace of God has appeared, bringing salvation to all men, instructing us that, having denied ungodliness and worldly desires, we should live soberly and righteously and godly in the present age.” - Titus 2:11–12, BLB

Grace trains believers to deny.

That word has almost disappeared from modern Christian speech. We hear constantly that grace receives, restores, comforts, and assures. All of that is true. Paul also says grace instructs believers to reject worldly desires and live soberly in the present age. A theology of grace that never trains anyone to say no has cut Paul’s sentence in half.

The same pattern appears in 1 Corinthians 9, where Paul compares the Christian life to athletic preparation. Runners exercise restraint because they want a perishable crown. Paul says Christians should run for an imperishable one:

“Every one striving exercises self-control in all things. Therefore those indeed, that they might receive a perishable crown; but we, an imperishable.” - 1 Corinthians 9:25, BLB

Then his language becomes physical:

“But I batter my body and bring it into servitude, lest having preached to others, I myself should be disqualified.” - 1 Corinthians 9:27, BLB

Paul does not assume the body becomes trustworthy after conversion. He treats it as something requiring government. Desire must be trained. Appetite must be restrained. The body must learn obedience through repeated refusal.

Peter gives the same picture of active growth:

“And for this very reason also, having applied all diligence, supply in your faith virtue, and in virtue knowledge, and in knowledge self-control, and in self-control perseverance, and in perseverance godliness, and in godliness brotherly affection, and in brotherly affection love.” - 2 Peter 1:5–7, BLB

Faith is the beginning of a cultivated life. Virtue, knowledge, self-control, perseverance, godliness, brotherly affection, and love are to be supplied with diligence. Peter then says these qualities keep believers from becoming ineffective and unfruitful in the knowledge of Christ.

“For these things being in you and abounding, make you neither idle nor unfruitful as to the knowledge of our Lord Jesus Christ.” - 2 Peter 1:8 (BLB)

He does not imagine maturity appearing automatically while Christians consume religious material. Growth requires attention, effort, repetition, and endurance.

Titus 2:6 makes the expectation painfully direct:

“Likewise, exhort the younger men to be self-controlled.” - Titus 2:6, BLB

Young men are not treated as creatures who should be entertained until their hormones calm down. They are commanded to govern themselves.

Much of modern youth ministry has worked from the opposite assumption. It lowers expectations, surrounds young men with noise, and quietly accepts that serious discipline will come later. They are given games, slogans, emotional talks, and a few warnings about sex. Then they enter adulthood carrying bodies they were never taught to govern.

The New Testament sets a higher standard. Peter commands believers to be sober and vigilant because the adversary prowls like a roaring lion (1 Peter 5:8).

Jesus assumes His followers will fast and teaches them how to do it without performance (Matthew 6:16-18). Paul refuses to be mastered by anything (1 Corinthians 6:12). James demands control of the tongue (James 3:1-12). Hebrews praises those who endure under pressure and run with perseverance (Hebrews 10:36; 12:1).

The mature Christian described by the New Testament becomes increasingly difficult for lust, fear, anger, comfort, pressure, and appetite to command.

Modern Christianity has settled for someone who believes the correct things while remaining governable by everything else.

Conversion Became the Finish Line

Many Protestant churches became highly skilled at explaining how a sinner is justified and comparatively weak at explaining how a justified sinner is formed.

The conversion moment became the center of the whole Christian life. Pray the prayer. Answer the altar call. Gain assurance. Attend church. Consume teaching. Wait for heaven.

The New Testament treats conversion as entrance.

Baptism begins a life of obedience.

It does not graduate the believer from effort. Grace removes condemnation and establishes a new master. The person who once presented the body to sin now presents it to God as an instrument of righteousness (Romans 6:12-13).

Protestants were right to reject the idea that discipline earns salvation. Yet many communities wandered into the opposite error and began treating serious effort as spiritually suspicious.

Fasting felt Catholic. Rules felt legalistic. Bodily discipline sounded monastic. Repeated practices looked like dead religion. Anything measurable risked being called works-based.

The result was a strange form of Christianity where effort is accepted in nearly every part of life except spiritual formation.

A musician practices scales. An athlete trains the body. A soldier drills under pressure. A recovering addict builds structure around weakness. A student repeats difficult material until knowledge becomes usable. Christians understand that repetition forms ability everywhere else. Then they enter church and are told that spiritual maturity will somehow emerge from hearing enough sermons.

Works do not save. Discipline does not purchase grace. God is not placed in anyone’s debt because a believer fasted, woke early, controlled his speech, or resisted temptation. Discipline is the trained response of a person who has received grace and now seeks to live under its instruction.

Paul captures the order clearly:

“Work out your own salvation with fear and trembling, for it is God who works in you both to will and to work according to His good pleasure.” - Philippians 2:12–13, BLB

God works in the believer.

The believer works.

Paul does not see a contradiction.

Modern Christians do because grace has been reduced to pardon while salvation has been reduced to destination. The biblical work is larger. Christ saves people from guilt, slavery, corruption, disordered desire, and obedience to the flesh. Salvation carries the person into a new kind of life.

A faith that never teaches the body to obey has misunderstood what salvation is saving a person into.

When Every Demand Became Legalism

“Legalism” has become one of the most abused words in Protestant culture.

Actual legalism is real. It places human rules where God did not. It treats performance as the ground of acceptance. It burdens consciences beyond Scripture. It turns discipline into a ladder by which people imagine they can climb into God’s favor.

Modern Christians use the same word for any expectation that interrupts comfort.

Fast regularly, and someone warns about legalism.

Control food, order sleep, resist sexual fantasy, keep commitments, govern time, deny yourself comforts, and the language of grace quickly appears as a shield against obedience.

The flesh has learned Christian vocabulary.

It no longer needs to argue that appetite should rule. It only needs to accuse discipline of legalism.

Paul’s definition of freedom leaves no room for this:

“All things are lawful for me, but not all things are profitable. All things are lawful for me, but I will not be mastered by anything.” - 1 Corinthians 6:12, BLB

Christian liberty means the believer is free to obey God without being ruled by sin, appetite, fear, or human tradition. It does not mean every desire receives a hearing. A person who cannot refuse food, screens, sex, anger, shopping, entertainment, or comfort is not walking in freedom merely because no church rule stopped him.

He is being mastered.

The question is simple: when did telling a Christian to govern his appetites become more dangerous than allowing his appetites to govern him?

A church terrified of legalism can become so permissive that the flesh rules without ever needing to defend itself. Everything is forgiven in advance. Nothing is trained. The believer remains trapped, but the trap has been renamed grace.

The Devotional Church

Devotionals are not inherently shallow. A strong devotional can direct the mind toward Scripture, expose sin, strengthen attention, and support a serious life of obedience. The problem begins when devotional consumption becomes a substitute for formation.

The format is perfect for modern religious life. It is brief, repeatable, emotionally manageable, easy to produce, easy to sell, and easy to complete. A reader receives a verse, a reflection, a comforting line, and perhaps a question for the day. Ten minutes later, the box is checked.

Formation asks harder questions.

What time do you wake?

What controls your attention?

What happens when desire rises?

Can you remain silent when anger wants the last word?

Can you fast without turning the fast into performance?

Can you work after enthusiasm dies?

Can you endure boredom without reaching for stimulation?

Can you keep a promise when obedience becomes inconvenient?

Can you refuse pleasure when the body demands relief?

A devotional can deliver a thought. Discipline builds a person.

The devotional industry can give Christians a fresh paragraph every morning while leaving the same appetites on the throne every night. The reader feels movement because new words keep arriving. The habits remain untouched.

This is one reason end-times speculation becomes so attractive. Prophecy offers drama, hidden knowledge, patterns, enemies, urgency, and the thrill of understanding what others missed.

Self-control offers no spectacle. It tells a man to close the screen, govern his mouth, refuse fantasy, stop blaming others, work quietly, pray without applause, endure discomfort, and remain faithful when nothing dramatic happens.

It is easier to identify the “end times” than to identify the appetite ruling your own body.

A man can spend twenty years watching for the mark of the beast while never noticing what already masters him.

Scripture contains prophecy, and Christians should study it. Jesus and the apostles repeatedly command watchfulness. Yet biblical watchfulness produces sobriety, endurance, faithfulness, and readiness. Modern prophecy culture can produce the opposite. People become agitated, speculative, suspicious, and addicted to updates while remaining unprepared for ordinary temptation.

Why are believers trained to decode future persecution while barely trained to endure present temptation?

A faith obsessed with escape will neglect the muscles required for endurance. The New Testament prepares Christians to remain faithful under pressure. It teaches patience, sobriety, vigilance, courage, and perseverance. Prophecy that does not form those qualities becomes religious entertainment.

Prophecy without formation produces informed cowards.

One Hour Against the Appetite Machine

The weakness often begins in childhood.

Sunday school teaches biblical stories, simplified moral lessons, memory verses, crafts, songs, and isolated examples of obedience. Children learn that Daniel refused the king’s food, Joseph fled sexual temptation, Jesus fasted, David faced Goliath, and the apostles endured persecution.

They are rarely shown how refusal becomes a habit.

They hear that Daniel exercised discipline without being trained to practice any. They hear that Jesus fasted without ever being expected to fast. They learn that Joseph fled lust while devices capable of delivering endless sexual corruption are placed into their hands with almost no preparation.

A growing Christian rule of life is usually absent.

Children are not systematically trained in patience, delayed gratification, truthful speech, control of anger, stewardship of attention, bodily purity, silence, service, responsibility, endurance, resistance to peer pressure, and completion of difficult work. They receive heroes of discipline inside churches that expect almost none from them.

The church may get one hour.

The phone, entertainment system, advertising industry, pornography economy, peer group, and consumer culture train appetite all week. Every notification rewards interruption. Every platform removes boredom. Every advertisement feeds dissatisfaction. Food arrives instantly. Sexual stimulation arrives instantly. Anger finds an audience instantly. Purchases arrive with a tap.

A weekly lesson cannot defeat a daily liturgy of indulgence.

The church and household must build counter-habits. Children need opportunities to wait, work, serve, remain quiet, finish tasks, control speech, accept correction, and go without. They need adults who practice the same things. Discipline taught without example becomes another sermon floating above real life.

The modern church treats children as consumers before they are old enough to name the transaction. Keep them entertained. Hold their attention. Make the lesson exciting. Remove friction. Avoid boredom. Reward attendance.

Then everyone acts surprised when they become adults who expect faith to remain entertaining.

The Consumer Church

Churches operate under real pressures. They need attendance, giving, volunteers, retention, cooperation, and some measure of public trust. Those pressures create incentives even when no leader consciously decides to build a consumer church.

Messages about purpose, breakthrough, blessing, encouragement, destiny, reassurance, and personal significance produce immediate emotional reward. Messages about fasting, restraint, repentance, endurance, and self-denial produce resistance.

A church does not need to choose consumer Christianity openly. It only needs to keep rewarding whatever causes the least resistance.

Over time, the congregation becomes an audience. The service is judged by whether it held attention, met needs, encouraged people, and gave them something useful. The sermon becomes content. Worship becomes experience. Fellowship becomes networking. Discipleship becomes another optional program for the motivated.

Consumers ask whether the church met their needs.

Disciples ask what obedience now requires.

Jesus never built His call around customer satisfaction. He told people to count the cost. He warned that following Him could divide households, expose loyalties, demand possessions, and lead to suffering. He sent disciples into a hostile world with no promise that obedience would feel convenient.

The modern church fears that such demands will drive people away.

Jesus allowed people to walk.

Low expectations do not produce mercy.

They produce weak disciples.

Information Without Apprenticeship

Modern Christians possess unprecedented access to information. Sermons from thousands of pastors are available instantly. Bible software can compare translations, languages, manuscripts, and commentaries in seconds. Courses, conferences, reading plans, clips, podcasts, and devotional libraries never stop growing.

Maturity has not grown at the same pace.

The reason is plain. Knowledge and formation are different works.

A person can know fasting is biblical without fasting. He can know lust is sinful without fleeing it. He can know anger is dangerous without controlling his speech. He can know prayer matters without ordering his day around it. He can know endurance is required without practicing discomfort.

The modern church has confused exposure to truth with submission to truth.

The secular world has rediscovered much of what churches stopped teaching. Psychology speaks about impulse control, emotional regulation, delayed gratification, distress tolerance, compulsive behavior, environmental shaping, and attention management. Sports culture understands training. Military culture understands readiness. Recovery programs understand structure. Serious artists understand repetition. Businesses understand delayed reward.

Psychology calls it impulse control. Sports calls it training. Recovery calls it sobriety. Scripture was already calling it self-control.

Behavioral science can describe how habits form and how environments shape action. It can show why immediate rewards overpower distant goals and why repeated cues become automatic responses. It cannot tell us what the human body is for, whom it belongs to, or why mastery matters.

Scripture gives the purpose.

The body belongs to God.

“Present your bodies as a living sacrifice, holy, well-pleasing to God, which is your reasonable service.” - Romans 12:1, BLB

That verse removes the body from private ownership. Appetite does not decide how the sacrifice is used. Emotion does not become revelation. Desire does not gain authority because it is strong.

Christianity does not teach hatred of the body. It teaches that the body is too important to be abandoned to appetite.

What Formation Would Require

A church serious about formation would teach fasting and practice it. Believers would learn why Christians fast, how to begin, how to avoid performance, and how hunger exposes dependence. Fasting would stop being an ancient curiosity mentioned during sermons about Jesus.

It would teach stewardship of attention. Christians would learn to impose limits on phones, entertainment, and constant stimulation. Silence would return as a discipline. Scripture reading would demand sustained attention rather than another stream of fragments between notifications.

It would speak plainly about sleep, food, sexuality, work, rest, and the refusal to be mastered. The body would be treated as part of discipleship rather than transportation for the soul.

Speech would receive serious attention. Gossip, slander, impulsive anger, lying, complaint, and the need to answer every insult would be treated as failures of self-government. James says the person who controls the tongue can govern the whole body (James 3:2). Churches would build cultures where restraint is admired more than verbal dominance.

Believers would be prepared for endurance. They would learn how to remain faithful through boredom, delay, grief, unanswered questions, opposition, and slow growth. Spiritual life would stop being measured by emotional intensity.

Confession and accountability would become ordinary without becoming surveillance. Weakness could be named before it became a hidden kingdom. Christians would have relationships where someone could ask about food, lust, money, anger, screens, sleep, and unfinished commitments without the question feeling invasive.

Children and teenagers would receive age-appropriate formation. They would learn how Christians practice restraint, keep promises, control speech, fast in suitable ways, serve without applause, and resist the liturgies built into their devices.

Churches would help believers establish simple rules of life: prayer, Scripture, fasting, work, service, rest, examination, and community arranged into repeatable rhythms. This requires no monastic costume and no imported personality. It requires life ordered around obedience.

The church does not need another mountain of content.

It needs Christians who have practiced obedience long enough for truth to enter their reflexes.

The Question Protestants Must Face

Has fear of works made you suspicious of effort?

Has assurance become an excuse to avoid examining fruit?

Do you know more about prophecy than your own habits?

Have you mistaken consuming Christian material for being formed by Christ?

Can you fast?

Can you control your speech?

Can you refuse sexual fantasy?

Can you endure boredom without reaching for stimulation?

Can you obey when you do not feel spiritually motivated?

What appetite currently holds more practical authority over you than Scripture?

The Protestant reader does not need to become Catholic, Orthodox, or monastic to recover self-control. He needs to stop skipping the parts of his own New Testament that demand it.

Paul names self-control as fruit.

Fruit is visible. It tells you what the tree is producing.

A church may have accurate sermons, crowded events, elaborate prophecy systems, emotional worship, and endless devotional material.

If its people remain enslaved to appetite, something has gone wrong in the field.

The New Testament never promises maturity through information alone. It commands believers to watch, endure, fast, resist, train, remain sober, and bring the body under obedience.

Modern Christianity has spent years teaching believers how to feel assured while barely teaching them how to become governable.

The result is a church that can discuss the end of the world but cannot end an appetite.

Self-control is no fringe discipline for unusually serious Christians. Paul calls it fruit of the Spirit.

A church overflowing with teaching should no longer be satisfied with producing people who were never trained to tell themselves no.

Kingdom Code is building a formation archive for Christians who want more than another devotional thought. Inside the Archive, I’m developing deeper studies on fasting, self-control, attention, bodily discipline, endurance, and the practices Scripture expects believers to recover.
